title: SIU clears police of any wrongdoing related to death of Bruce Frogg
article: Ontario's police watchdog says the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) did not commit any crimes by fatally subduing a 57-year-old man at Anicinabe Park in Kenora last year.

Shortly after noon on Tuesday, June 24, 2024, Bruce Frogg, a man from Wawakapewin First Nation arrived at the Anicinabe Park campground in Kenora "in a highly agitated state," and according to witnesses, he poured gas or oil on both himself and the exterior of the park's office and convenience store before setting a shopping cart full of wood he brought with him on fire.

As the building went up in flames and the lone employee inside fled, the OPP arrived on the scene approximately five minutes later, by which point Frogg was wielding a meat cleaver in each hand. Despite the responding officer asking him to drop the knives, Frogg refused, allegedly saying that "no one helped him."

By 12:08 p.m., several more officers had arrived on the scene, including with a rifle and a tactical K9 unit, to form a perimeter around the suspect while the building burned. While the original responding officer pleaded with Frogg let go of the weapons, he " refused and challenged the officers to shoot him" while at times "banging (the knives) off the deck balcony's railing."

Not long after into the standoff, local firefighters also arrived, and "it was hoped that the water would, directly or indirectly, whether by distracting (Frogg) or causing him to lose balance, permit the officers an opportunity to safely take the (him) into custody."

When the water " struck him indirectly and began to create mist or steam in his area," Frogg - who had removed his shirt at some point - walked forward into the parking lot toward the police, resulting in a second officer firing three times. Frogg was subsequently handcuffed and provided with emergency medical aid, but was pronounced deceased at the Lake of the Woods District Hospital later in the afternoon.

This information is the summary of the official report released by Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) on July 2, and according to SIU Director Joseph Martino, "t here are no reasonable grounds to believe that either officer committed a criminal offence in connection with (Frogg's) death."

According to Martino, the police "w ere lawfully placed and in the execution of their duties through the events that culminated in the shooting" and "they were duty-bound to respond to the scene to do what they reasonably could to ensure public safety."

In the eyes of the SIU, Frogg's approach toward the police, and the police's gunfire response constituted " reasonable force" and a " reasonably apprehended attack," based largely on Frogg's wielding of two cleavers and "his volatile behaviour to that point."
"The officers on scene . . . conducted themselves with due care and regard for public safety, including (Frogg's) health and well-being," Martino wrote as part of his July 2 decision.

"They were confronted by an emergency situation, the fire having already been started by the time the first officers arrived on scene. From the get-go, officers spoke to (Frogg) to have him drop the knives and distance himself from a burning building."
In making his decision, Martino called the incident a " tragic turn of events" and noted that the police "had a difficult decision to make and not much time in which to make it."

There were a total of 26 witnesses attached to the investigation (although one of them declined to be interviewed). The SIU has also written that an " internal administrative error" caused an investigative delay with the case, which was released more than a year after the original date of the incident.

Smartphone footage, as well as video evidence recorded from both the Anicinabe Park office and OPP vehicles were used to help investigate the incident. Toxicology reports and the deceased's postmortem file were also obtained by the SIU to help build the incident narrative.

At the time, Frogg's death was controversial to say the least, as several First Nations leaders - including Kiiwetinoong's Member of Provincial Parliament Sol Mamakwa, Grand Council Treaty #3 Grand Chiefs Francis Kavanaugh, and Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN) Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler - officially called " for accountability after (the) tragic shooting, " with some going so far as to say First Nations have a "broken relationship" with the police .
The future of Anicinabe Park itself remains up in the air, as three First Nations remain in the process of suing both the City of Kenora and the Government of Canada for the "return" of the land .
